blocks.content: ConfigMap solved configuration for values that are fine to see in a manifest diff. Passwords, tokens, and keys are not those values. This topic covers the object built specifically for the data that genuinely must not leak.
Secrets, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Secrets, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: A Secret is a Kubernetes object structurally almost identical to a ConfigMap, storing key value pairs, but specifically intended for sensitive data such as passwords, API tokens, TLS private keys, and other credentials an application needs.

Like a ConfigMap, a Secret is created declaratively, stored in etcd, and referenced by Pods through the exact same consumption methods, environment variables, volume mounts, or command arguments, all covered as their own topics in this module.

The genuinely meaningful difference from ConfigMap lies in how Kubernetes treats a Secret internally and in the additional handling conventions built around it, both of which are the direct focus of this topic's full, dedicated depth.

Understanding Secrets correctly, including precisely what protection they do and do not provide, is essential for handling credentials safely in any real Kubernetes cluster running genuine production workloads.

blocks.content: Base64 Encoding Is Not Encryption

By default, a Secret's values are stored in etcd encoded using base64, a reversible, non secret encoding scheme, not an encryption algorithm, meaning anyone with read access to the raw Secret object can trivially decode its values back to plain text.

This is a genuinely important, frequently misunderstood distinction: base64 encoding exists purely to safely represent arbitrary binary data as text within a YAML or JSON manifest, not to provide any actual confidentiality protection for that data.

Kubernetes's role based access control, restricting which users and service accounts can read Secret objects at all, is the primary real protection mechanism, not the base64 encoding itself, which should be assumed fully and trivially reversible by anyone who can see it.

Recognizing this distinction clearly prevents a dangerous false sense of security, where a team assumes a Secret's contents are genuinely protected simply because they appear as a jumble of base64 characters rather than obviously readable plain text.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731611394-843295390.png
blocks.alt: A base64 encoded value is genuinely not the same thing as encryption

blocks.content: A Real Secret Example

Consider a database password an application needs to connect to its backing datastore, genuinely sensitive data that should never appear in plain text within a version controlled manifest or a container image.

A Secret named db-credentials holds a key such as DB_PASSWORD, with its value base64 encoded within the manifest, and the application's Pod spec references this Secret exactly the way a ConfigMap would be referenced, through the same consumption mechanisms.

Kubernetes's role based access control is then configured to restrict which users and service accounts can actually read this Secret object, ensuring only the application itself, and specifically authorized human operators, can access the real password value.

This combination, a Secret object plus deliberately configured access control, is what genuinely protects the credential, not the base64 encoding alone, which is precisely the distinction this topic's earlier section established in detail.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
type: Opaque
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXRwYXNzd29yZA==

blocks.content: Recap: The Same API Shape, One Critical Difference
blocks.text: Recap: The Same API Shape, One Critical Difference

blocks.content: The previous topic covered ConfigMap in full, establishing a key value object referenced by Pods through environment variables, volume mounts, or command arguments, stored declaratively in etcd exactly like every other Kubernetes object.

Secret shares essentially that entire same shape and consumption model, which is precisely why so much of what was learned about ConfigMap transfers directly and immediately to working with Secrets without needing to relearn the mechanics from scratch.

The one critical difference is sensitivity, and everything this topic covers, base64 versus encryption, access control, and encryption at rest, exists specifically to address the real, practical consequences of that one difference.
Approaching Secrets as ConfigMap plus sensitivity handling, rather than as an entirely separate, unrelated object, is the correct and most efficient way to build genuine fluency with it quickly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731614953-977324301.png
blocks.alt: Recap of ConfigMap, already covered, sharing the same API shape

blocks.content: Encryption at Rest for etcd

Kubernetes supports configuring encryption at rest specifically for Secret data stored in etcd, meaning the actual bytes written to etcd's own underlying storage are genuinely encrypted, not merely base64 encoded, protecting against direct access to etcd's storage files.

This encryption at rest is an optional cluster level configuration, not enabled by default on many Kubernetes distributions, and enabling it is a meaningful, recommended hardening step for any cluster handling genuinely sensitive production credentials.

Managed cloud Kubernetes offerings frequently provide this encryption at rest as a configurable option, or occasionally as an always on default, and confirming its status is a worthwhile check for any team operating a production cluster.

This is the piece of the picture that finally does provide genuine confidentiality at the storage layer, complementing rather than replacing the role based access control already covered as the primary protection for who can read a Secret through the API itself.

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Assuming Secrets Are Automatically Secure
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Assuming Secrets Are Automatically Secure

blocks.content: A common and genuinely risky mistake is assuming that simply using a Secret object, rather than a ConfigMap, automatically provides strong security for sensitive data, without configuring role based access control or encryption at rest deliberately.

A Secret with no restrictive access control configured is readable by any user or service account with general read access to that namespace, which in a loosely configured cluster can be a considerably larger group than the team might assume.

This mistake is genuinely dangerous specifically because it feels secure. The object is literally named Secret, and its values are visibly base64 encoded rather than plain text, both of which create a false, misleading sense of protection.

The fix is deliberate: treat a Secret object as one necessary piece of a larger security posture, always paired with genuinely restrictive role based access control and, ideally, encryption at rest configured explicitly at the cluster level.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731618207-916195382.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of assuming a Secret object is automatically secure

blocks.content: Immutable Secrets, Mirroring ConfigMap

Just as a ConfigMap can be marked immutable, a Secret supports the exact same immutable field, preventing further changes to its data after creation and requiring a new, distinctly named Secret object for any update instead.

This is genuinely valuable for credentials that should never be casually edited in place, since an immutable Secret forces any rotation to go through a deliberate, explicit process of creating a new object and updating references to it.

The performance benefit already covered for ConfigMap applies equally here: an immutable Secret reduces API server watch load, which matters proportionally more for Secrets given how frequently they are read by many Pods across a cluster.

Combining immutability with a clear credential rotation process, covered later in this topic, gives a genuinely robust, auditable way to manage sensitive values through their full lifecycle rather than editing them quietly in place.
Secret Rotation in Practice

Rotating a credential, replacing an old password or token with a new one on a regular schedule or after a suspected compromise, is a standard security practice that Kubernetes Secrets support directly through the same update mechanisms already covered.

For a mutable Secret consumed as a mounted volume, updating its value propagates to running Pods automatically, similarly to the ConfigMap volume behavior covered earlier, letting an application pick up a rotated credential without requiring a restart in many cases.

For a mutable Secret consumed as an environment variable, exactly as covered for ConfigMap, a Pod restart is required to actually pick up the rotated value, since environment variables are fixed at container startup time and never automatically refresh.

Building a reliable, tested rotation process before it is genuinely needed, rather than improvising one during an active security incident, is a meaningful piece of operational maturity worth investing in for any cluster handling real production credentials.

blocks.title: Operational Note
blocks.content: Test credential rotation deliberately, before an incident forces it. Confirm whether the consuming application actually picks up a rotated Secret automatically or requires an explicit restart.
Secrets and Service Accounts

Every Pod runs under a service account, and historically, Kubernetes automatically mounted a Secret containing that service account's authentication token into every Pod by default, a pattern that has since evolved toward more time bound, automatically rotated tokens.

This service account token mechanism is a specialized, automatically managed use of the same underlying Secret machinery covered throughout this topic, though it is handled largely invisibly by Kubernetes itself rather than something an application team typically manages directly.

Understanding that service account tokens are, underneath, genuinely Secret objects helps connect this topic to the Security module covered later in this course, where service accounts and their associated permissions receive their own full, dedicated depth.

For now, it is enough to recognize this connection exists. The practical details of service account permissions and token management are covered fully once the Security module is reached later in this course.
Comparing Kubernetes Secrets to External Secret Stores
blocks.text: Comparing Kubernetes Secrets to External Secret Stores

blocks.content: Kubernetes's built in Secret object stores data directly in etcd, protected by access control and optional encryption at rest, while an external secret store, such as Vault, keeps the authoritative value entirely outside etcd, injecting it only at Pod startup time.

The external store approach offers stronger guarantees in some respects, such as centralized audit logging across every consuming application and short lived, automatically expiring credentials, at the cost of additional infrastructure to operate and integrate.

For many teams, particularly smaller ones without a dedicated security or platform team, Kubernetes's built in Secret object, combined with the practices covered throughout this topic, is a genuinely sufficient, pragmatic starting point.

Recognizing this as a spectrum of increasing security sophistication, rather than a binary choice, helps a team correctly judge when their own credential handling needs have genuinely outgrown the built in Secret object alone.

External Secret Management Integration

Many production clusters integrate with an external, dedicated secret management system, such as HashiCorp Vault or a cloud provider's own secret manager, rather than relying solely on Kubernetes's own built in Secret object for the most sensitive credentials.

These integrations typically work through a controller or a mutating admission mechanism that fetches the real secret value from the external system at Pod startup time, injecting it into the container without that value ever being persisted directly in etcd at all.

This pattern adds genuine additional security benefits, such as centralized audit logging of every secret access and fine grained, short lived credential issuance, beyond what Kubernetes's own built in Secret object provides on its own.

For many teams, especially smaller ones, Kubernetes's built in Secret object, combined with careful access control and encryption at rest, is entirely sufficient, and external secret management is a deliberate upgrade reserved for higher security requirements.
Auditing Secret Access

Kubernetes audit logging, when enabled at the cluster level, records every request made to the API server, including every read of a Secret object, providing a genuine, reviewable trail of exactly who or what accessed sensitive credentials and when.

Reviewing this audit trail periodically, or configuring automated alerting on unusual Secret access patterns, is a genuinely valuable operational practice for any cluster handling credentials with real, meaningful consequences if compromised.

This auditing capability is a direct extension of the broader Kubernetes API server behavior already covered in the Architecture module earlier in this course, where every single object interaction passes through and can be logged by that same central component.

Building this kind of visibility into standard operational practice, rather than only reaching for it reactively after an incident has already occurred, is a meaningful maturity step for any team responsible for a real production cluster.

blocks.title: Operational Note
blocks.content: Enable and review Kubernetes audit logging for Secret access on any cluster handling credentials with real consequences if compromised.
Best Practices for Secrets

Never commit a Secret manifest containing real, unencrypted base64 values directly to source control. Use a secret management integration, a sealed secrets tool, or a deliberate manual application process instead of plain YAML in a repository.

Configure role based access control restrictively for every Secret, granting read access only to the specific service accounts and human operators that genuinely need it, rather than relying on broad, default namespace level permissions.

Enable encryption at rest for etcd on any cluster handling genuinely sensitive production credentials, treating it as a standard, expected piece of cluster hardening rather than an optional, advanced configuration.

Rotate sensitive credentials periodically, and immediately upon any suspected compromise, treating a Secret's value as something with a genuine lifecycle rather than a value set once at cluster creation and left unchanged indefinitely.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

A Secret object shares nearly its entire shape with ConfigMap, but the one difference, sensitivity, changes everything about how it must actually be handled: access control and encryption at rest matter, and base64 alone provides no real protection.

Treating a Secret as automatically secure simply because of its name is the single most dangerous misunderstanding covered in this topic, and avoiding it requires deliberate, explicit security configuration, not passive trust in the object type alone.

The next topic, Environment Variables, covers the first of the two consumption mechanisms already previewed in the ConfigMap topic, applying equally to both ConfigMap and Secret data delivered into a running container.

Keep the encoding versus encryption distinction firmly in mind. It is the single fact about Secrets most likely to be misunderstood, and correctly understanding it is the foundation everything else in this topic builds on.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: access control and encryption at rest are not optional extras layered on top of a Secret. They are the actual security mechanism, with the object itself providing structure alone.
Secrets is now fully covered; Environment Variables, the first shared delivery mechanism for both objects, follows immediately next.
